claims.text: Controlled biaxial strain imposed during deposition changes the energy landscape of the FeMnNiGeSi magnetostructural transition.
Biaxial strain reduces the abruptness of the first-order transition.
Biaxial strain reduces hysteresis by partially decoupling magnetic and structural order parameters.
Arc-melted or melt-spun non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys form a single-phase hexagonal structure with a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
Depositing films on substrates with different lattice mismatches can impose systematically controlled biaxial strain.
The substrate-based intervention tailors microstructural and magnetic-anisotropy characteristics.
Annealing at 300–500 °C for short durations in an inert atmosphere will stabilize the strained microstructure.
The relevant magnetostructural transition occurs around room temperature.
Substrate-induced biaxial strain and the resulting nanocrystalline grain/matrix structure modify coupling between magnetic and structural order parameters.
Imposed strain alters local lattice parameters and magnetic anisotropy.
Changes in lattice parameters and magnetic anisotropy smooth the transition's free-energy barrier.
Smoothing the free-energy barrier diminishes the abrupt, strongly coupled magnetostructural change and produces a broader, less hysteretic response.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of thin films promotes more uniform nucleation and growth of the new phase.
Strained thin films will have a slightly broadened magnetocaloric transition peak relative to the strain-free baseline.
Strained thin films will have reduced hysteresis and lower energy loss per cycle relative to the strain-free baseline.
Thin films will have improved heat-exchange kinetics because of their higher surface area.
Arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons have limited heat exchange because of low surface-to-volume ratio.
The predicted mechanism applies to 50–200 nm films under moderate annealing and 0.1–1 T cycling near room temperature, but may not transfer to bulk polycrystalline forms.
A lack of statistically significant strain-dependent change in both hysteresis and magnetocaloric entropy change relative to lattice-matched film controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state is called 'as-deposited' while being defined as arc-melted or melt-spun material, whereas the intervention and boundary use deposition to mean physical-vapor-deposited thin films. These are materially different processing routes and comparator states.
The target is described as as-deposited, but the proposed conditions include post-deposition annealing. Unless an unannealed arm is retained, the tested state is no longer strictly as-deposited.

The predicted outcome invokes an as-deposited, strain-free baseline; the baseline field instead specifies ingots or microribbons, while the falsification design uses nearly lattice-matched thin films. These non-equivalent controls confound strain with geometry, deposition route, and annealing history.
